title: The CIA triad
hook: The three goals every security control serves: keep data secret, correct and available.
what: Security has three core goals, the CIA triad. Confidentiality means only the right people can see data (passwords, encryption, access control). Integrity means data is correct and hasn't been tampered with (hashes, digital signatures, change control). Availability means systems are up when people need them (backups, redundancy, DDoS protection). Almost every control you'll meet protects one or more of these, and they can pull against each other: locking something down tightly (confidentiality) can make it harder to reach (availability).

example.title: Ransomware hits all three
example.text: A ransomware attack is a neat illustration: encrypting the files destroys availability, stealing a copy first breaks confidentiality, and altering or deleting data breaks integrity. That's why it's treated as a top business risk, not just an IT problem.

defend: Confidentiality: encryption, strong authentication and least-privilege access
Integrity: hashing, digital signatures, input validation and change management
Availability: tested backups, redundancy, capacity planning and DDoS protection
Balance the three: the right level depends on what the data is worth

checks.q: Which part of the CIA triad does encrypting a file protect?
checks.why: Encryption keeps data secret, so only someone with the key can read it. That's confidentiality.

checks.q: A website is knocked offline by a flood of traffic. Which goal has been attacked?
checks.why: If people can't reach the system when they need it, availability has failed. A DDoS attacks availability.

checks.q: You compare a downloaded file's hash to the published one and they match. What have you confirmed?
checks.why: A matching hash shows the file is unchanged, which is integrity. (Proving who made it needs a signature.)

concept.title: The three goals every control serves

items.label: Confidentiality
items.text: Only the right people can see the data. Built with encryption, authentication and least-privilege access.
items.example: A leaked customer database breaks confidentiality — outsiders can now read private data.

items.label: Integrity
items.text: Data is correct and hasn't been tampered with. Built with hashing, digital signatures and change control.
items.example: A matching file hash proves the download wasn't altered in transit.

items.label: Availability
items.text: Systems are up when people need them. Built with backups, redundancy and DDoS protection.
items.example: A DDoS attack that knocks a site offline is an attack on availability.

title: Security frameworks & governance
hook: The playbooks organisations use to decide what to protect and how.
what: A security framework is a structured set of good practices so organisations don't have to invent security from scratch. The NIST Cybersecurity Framework groups work into six functions: Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond and Recover. ISO 27001 is an international standard for running an information security management system. MITRE ATT&CK catalogues how real attackers behave, so defenders can check their coverage. Governance is the layer above the tools: policies, risk decisions and making sure rules are actually followed. Compliance (meeting rules like GDPR, HIPAA or PCI DSS) overlaps with security but isn't the same thing: you can be compliant and still insecure.

example.title: The NIST CSF in practice
example.text: When a company says it is 'mapping to the NIST CSF', it means checking each function: do we know what we have (Identify)? Can we stop attacks (Protect) and spot them (Detect)? Do we have a plan to Respond and Recover? The newest version added Govern to put risk ownership at the centre.

defend: Pick a framework that fits your size and sector rather than starting from nothing
Use MITRE ATT&CK to find gaps in what you can detect
Treat compliance as a floor, not the goal: meeting rules is not the same as being secure
Write policies people can actually follow, and review them

checks.q: What are the six functions of the NIST Cybersecurity Framework?
options: Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover
Plan, Do, Check, Act, Review, Repeat
Scan, Patch, Monitor, Alert, Block, Report
Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability, Audit, Comply, Insure
checks.why: The NIST CSF groups work into Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond and Recover.

checks.q: Which statement about compliance is true?
options: You can be compliant and still insecure
Compliance replaces the need for a framework
checks.why: Meeting rules like PCI DSS is a minimum bar; it doesn't guarantee you're actually secure.

checks.q: What is MITRE ATT&CK mainly used for?
options: Mapping real attacker tactics so defenders can find gaps
checks.why: ATT&CK catalogues how attackers behave, so teams can check what they would and wouldn't detect.

concept.title: The playbooks and who they serve

items.label: NIST CSF
items.text: Six functions — Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover — to organise a whole security programme.

items.label: ISO 27001
items.text: International standard for running an information security management system you can be certified against.

items.label: MITRE ATT&CK
items.text: A catalogue of real attacker tactics and techniques, used to find gaps in what you can detect.

items.label: Governance & compliance
items.text: Policies, risk ownership and meeting rules like GDPR or PCI DSS. Compliance is a floor, not a guarantee.

title: Phishing & social engineering
hook: Most breaches start with a message, not a hack.
what: Phishing is tricking someone into clicking a link, opening a file, handing over a password or sending money by pretending to be someone they trust. Social engineering is the wider skill of manipulating people: fake IT support calls (vishing), texts (smishing), or emails that impersonate the boss asking for an urgent payment (business email compromise). Attackers lean on urgency, authority and fear because people under pressure skip the checks they'd normally do.

example.title: MGM Resorts (Scattered Spider)
example.text: Attackers found an employee on LinkedIn, called the IT help desk pretending to be them, and talked staff into resetting their login. That one phone call led to ransomware that shut down hotel systems and cost MGM about $100 million.

defend: Phishing-resistant MFA (passkeys or security keys) so a stolen password isn't enough
Verify unusual requests through a second channel you already trust
Make reporting easy and never punish people for clicking
Email filtering plus SPF, DKIM and DMARC to block spoofed senders

checks.q: Your 'CEO' emails asking you to buy gift cards urgently and keep it quiet. What's the best move?
options: Buy them quickly, it's the CEO
Reply to the email to ask if it's real
Contact the CEO through a known phone number or chat
Forward it to colleagues to see what they think
checks.why: Replying goes straight back to the attacker. Verify through a channel you already trust.

checks.q: An email says your account will be closed within the hour unless you sign in now. Which trick is it mainly relying on?
checks.why: Attackers lean on urgency, authority and fear because people under pressure skip the checks they'd normally do.

checks.q: You typed your password into a fake login page. Which defence still stops the attacker getting in?
options: Phishing-resistant MFA such as a passkey or security key
checks.why: A passkey or security key only works on the real website, so a stolen password on its own isn't enough.

steps.msg: Email: “Your mailbox is full. Sign in to keep it.”
steps.text: The email looks like it comes from IT and adds urgency so the reader acts before thinking.
steps.stop: Email filtering and SPF, DKIM and DMARC catch many spoofed senders.

steps.msg: Clicks the link and types a password
steps.text: The link opens a copy of the real sign-in page on a lookalike address.
steps.stop: Check the address; report it. Never punish people who click.

steps.text: Whatever is typed into the fake page goes straight to the attacker.
With the password, the attacker logs in to the real account to read mail or phish colleagues from a trusted address.
steps.stop: Phishing-resistant MFA (passkeys) blocks this step: the password alone isn't enough.

title: Ransomware
hook: Encrypt everything, steal a copy, then demand payment twice.
what: Ransomware is malware that encrypts an organisation's files so they can't be used, then demands payment for the key. Modern gangs also steal the data first and threaten to publish it (double extortion). Most groups run as businesses: developers rent the ransomware to 'affiliates' who break in, often through stolen passwords, unpatched VPNs or phishing, then spend days quietly spreading before they strike.

example.title: Colonial Pipeline
example.text: Attackers logged in to an old VPN account with a leaked password and no MFA. The resulting ransomware attack shut down the largest fuel pipeline in the US for days and caused fuel shortages along the East Coast.

defend: Offline or immutable backups that are tested regularly
MFA on every remote access point (VPN, RDP, email)
Patch internet-facing systems first, especially anything on CISA's KEV list
Endpoint detection (EDR) and watching for mass file changes

practice.label: See free decryptors at No More Ransom

checks.q: Why aren't backups alone enough against modern ransomware?
options: Gangs also steal data and threaten to leak it
checks.why: Double extortion means restoring from backup doesn't stop the leak threat.

checks.q: In ransomware-as-a-service, who usually breaks into the victim's network?
checks.why: Developers rent the ransomware to affiliates, who break in, often with stolen passwords or unpatched VPNs, and spread before striking.

checks.q: Which backups are most likely to survive a ransomware attack?
options: A copy on the same server
Offline or immutable backups that are tested regularly
Backups on a mapped network drive
checks.why: Gangs hunt for reachable backups and destroy them. Offline or immutable copies can't be changed, and testing proves they actually restore.

diagram.title: How a ransomware attack reaches the point of encryption

steps.msg: Logs in with a stolen password
steps.text: Many attacks start at remote access: a reused password or an unpatched VPN.
steps.stop: MFA on every remote access point; patch internet-facing systems first.

steps.text: The attacker gains admin rights and maps the network before doing anything noisy.
steps.stop: Segment networks and give accounts only the access they need.

steps.text: Data is stolen first so the gang can threaten to leak it (double extortion).
steps.stop: Watch for unusual large outbound transfers.

steps.text: Gangs destroy backups they can reach so the victim can't simply restore.
steps.stop: Keep offline or immutable backups and test restoring them.

steps.msg: Encrypts files, leaves a ransom note
steps.text: Files become unusable and the ransom demand appears.
steps.stop: EDR that spots mass file changes can stop encryption early.

title: Malware families
hook: Trojans, worms, stealers, RATs: know what you're looking at.
what: Malware is any software built to cause harm. A trojan pretends to be something useful. A worm spreads by itself between machines. An infostealer grabs saved passwords, cookies and crypto wallets. A RAT (remote access trojan) gives the attacker control of your machine. A loader's only job is to download other malware. A botnet is thousands of infected devices taking orders from one controller.

example.title: WannaCry
example.text: A ransomware worm used a leaked NSA exploit (EternalBlue) to spread across unpatched Windows machines worldwide in hours, hitting the UK's NHS hard. Microsoft had released the patch two months earlier.

defend: Keep systems patched so worms have nowhere to spread
Only install software from trusted sources
Use EDR and application allow-listing
Don't let browsers store high-value passwords on shared machines

practice.label: Look up a file hash on VirusTotal

checks.q: Which malware type steals saved browser passwords and session cookies?
checks.why: Infostealers are a big driver of account takeovers because stolen cookies can bypass MFA.

checks.q: Which type of malware spreads between machines by itself, without anyone clicking anything?
checks.why: A worm spreads on its own, which is why keeping systems patched (leaving it nothing to exploit) matters so much.

checks.q: A program's only job is to download and run other malware. What is it?
checks.why: A loader fetches the next stage. Blocking it stops everything that would have followed.

items.label: Virus
items.text: Attaches to a file or program and spreads when that file is run by a person.

items.label: Worm
items.text: Spreads by itself across a network, with no user action, exploiting weaknesses.

items.label: Trojan
items.text: Disguised as something useful; the user installs it believing it's safe.

items.label: Ransomware
items.text: Encrypts files and demands payment; often steals a copy first to add pressure.

items.label: Spyware / infostealer
items.text: Quietly harvests passwords, cookies and keystrokes and sends them to the attacker.

items.label: Rootkit
items.text: Hides deep in the system to stay invisible and keep access across reboots.

items.label: Botnet
items.text: Many infected machines controlled together, rented out for spam or DDoS.

items.label: RAT
items.text: A remote-access trojan gives the attacker a hands-on backdoor into the machine.

title: Zero-days
hook: A bug the vendor has had zero days to fix.
what: A zero-day is a vulnerability attackers know about before the vendor does, so there's no patch yet. When it's being used in real attacks it's an 'in-the-wild zero-day'. They're rare and valuable, often used by nation-states or spyware vendors. Once a patch ships, it becomes an 'n-day', and the race is on: attackers reverse-engineer the patch while defenders try to install it.

example.title: Log4Shell
example.text: A flaw in Log4j, a logging library inside thousands of Java apps, let attackers run code just by getting a server to log a crafted string. It was exploited within hours of going public, and teams spent weeks just finding where Log4j was hiding.

defend: Know what software you run (an asset inventory and SBOM)
Layered defences so one bug isn't game over
Apply vendor mitigations quickly, before a patch exists
Monitor for unusual behaviour, not only known signatures

practice.label: Browse Google Project Zero's in-the-wild tracker

checks.q: When does a zero-day stop being a zero-day?
options: When the vendor releases a patch
When it gets a CVSS score
checks.why: Once a fix exists it's an n-day, but unpatched systems are still vulnerable.

checks.q: What is an 'n-day'?
options: A bug nobody has found yet
A vulnerability with no CVE ID
A known vulnerability that already has a patch
checks.why: Once a patch ships, a zero-day becomes an n-day: attackers study the patch while defenders race to install it.

checks.q: There's no patch yet for a zero-day in software you run. What helps most right now?
options: Apply the vendor's mitigations and watch for unusual behaviour
checks.why: Vendors often publish workarounds before a fix, and behaviour monitoring catches attacks that signatures miss.

items.label: Zero-day
items.text: A flaw the vendor doesn't know about yet — zero days to fix it. No patch exists.

items.label: In the wild
items.text: Attackers exploit it quietly before anyone defends against it. The most dangerous window.

items.label: Patch released
items.text: The vendor ships a fix once they learn of it. The race to install it begins.

items.label: N-day
items.text: After disclosure the flaw is public; unpatched systems are easy targets for everyone.

title: Vulnerabilities & patching
hook: CVE, CVSS, EPSS, KEV: how teams decide what to fix first.
what: Every public security bug gets a CVE ID. CVSS scores how bad it could be (0–10). EPSS estimates how likely it is to be exploited in the next 30 days. CISA's KEV list confirms which are being exploited right now. Tens of thousands of CVEs appear every year, far more than anyone can patch at once, so good teams prioritise by real-world risk: exploited first, likely next, then severity.

example.title: Equifax
example.text: A patch for a critical Apache Struts flaw was available for two months, but one internet-facing system wasn't updated. Attackers used it to steal personal data on about 147 million people.

defend: Keep an accurate inventory of systems and software
Patch KEV-listed and internet-facing issues first
Use EPSS alongside CVSS to cut the noise
Track time-to-patch as a team metric

practice.label: Explore this week's CVEs on the Radar

checks.q: A CVE has CVSS 6.5 and is on CISA's KEV list. Another has CVSS 9.8 with EPSS 0.2%. Which should most teams patch first?
options: The 6.5 on KEV, because it's being exploited
checks.why: Confirmed exploitation beats a theoretical worst case.

checks.q: What does EPSS estimate?
options: How severe a vulnerability could be
How likely a vulnerability is to be exploited in the next 30 days
How long a patch takes to install
checks.why: CVSS scores how bad a bug could be; EPSS estimates the chance it's exploited in the next 30 days.

checks.q: What does a CVE ID give you?
options: A unique name for one public vulnerability
checks.why: A CVE ID is a shared name so everyone means the same bug. Severity comes from CVSS, and exploitation from CISA's KEV list.

items.label: Identify
items.text: Scan and inventory. You can't fix what you don't know you have.

items.label: Prioritise
items.text: Rank by real risk — what's exploited now (KEV), exposed, and critical — not just raw severity.

items.label: Remediate
items.text: Patch, configure around it, or isolate it. Then move to the next most dangerous.

items.label: Verify
items.text: Re-scan to confirm the fix took, and feed what you learned back into the next round.

title: Supply chain attacks
hook: Why break in when you can ship inside a trusted update?
what: A supply chain attack compromises something many organisations trust (a software vendor, an update server, an open-source package or a managed service provider) so the attacker reaches all of their customers at once. Malicious npm and PyPI packages, typosquatted library names and hijacked maintainer accounts are now constant.

example.title: XZ Utils backdoor
example.text: Over two years, an attacker built trust as a helpful maintainer of a compression library used by Linux, then slipped in a backdoor targeting SSH. A Microsoft engineer spotted it because SSH logins were half a second slower than usual.

defend: Pin and verify dependencies; review what new packages do
Generate SBOMs so you can answer 'are we affected?' fast
Limit what build systems and vendors can access
Check signatures and provenance (frameworks like SLSA)

checks.q: What made the XZ Utils attack so dangerous?
options: It used a zero-click iPhone bug
A trusted maintainer inserted the backdoor
checks.why: Trust was the attack vector. Code review and reproducible builds are key defences.

checks.q: Why do attackers target software vendors and open-source packages?
options: One compromise reaches every organisation that trusts them
They're easier to find on the internet
checks.why: Compromising something many organisations trust lets an attacker reach all of its customers at once.

checks.q: What is typosquatting in package registries?
options: Publishing a malicious package named like a popular one
checks.why: Attackers publish packages with names one typo away from popular libraries, hoping a developer installs theirs by mistake.

items.label: Vendor updates
items.text: A trusted software update is laced with malware, so every customer installs it (SolarWinds).

items.label: Dependencies
items.text: A popular open-source package is poisoned; every project that pulls it in is affected.

items.label: Build pipeline
items.text: Attackers compromise the build system so malicious code is signed and shipped as genuine.

items.label: Third-party access
items.text: A supplier or MSP with a login into your network becomes the way in.

title: Data breaches
hook: Your data is probably already out there. Here's what that means.
what: A data breach is when information is accessed or taken by someone who shouldn't have it. It can be a hack, a misconfigured database left open to the internet, or an insider. Stolen data is sold, leaked or used for further attacks. Reused passwords from one breach get tried on other sites, which is called credential stuffing.

example.title: MOVEit
example.text: The Cl0p gang used a SQL injection zero-day in MOVEit Transfer, a file-sharing product, to steal data from over 2,700 organisations in one campaign, exposing personal data on roughly 93 million people.

defend: Collect and keep less data
Encrypt sensitive data and lock down database exposure
Unique passwords and a password manager for everyone
Monitor for leaked company credentials

practice.label: Check your email on Have I Been Pwned

checks.q: What is credential stuffing?
options: Guessing passwords one letter at a time
Trying leaked username/password pairs on other sites
Putting too many passwords in a manager
checks.why: It works because people reuse passwords. Unique passwords stop it.

checks.q: Which of these is a data breach?
options: A stranger downloads a customer database that was left open to the internet
A website goes offline for an hour
checks.why: A breach is any access to data by someone who shouldn't have it. Misconfigured, exposed databases count, not only hacks.

checks.q: What stops credential stuffing from working on your accounts?
options: A different password for every site, kept in a password manager
checks.why: Credential stuffing replays passwords leaked from one site on others, so it only works when a password is reused.

items.label: Stolen credentials
items.text: Reused or phished passwords let attackers log in as a real user — the most common route.

items.label: Misconfiguration
items.text: An exposed database or storage bucket left open to the internet with no password.

items.label: Unpatched flaw
items.text: A known vulnerability that was never fixed gives attackers a way in.

items.label: Phishing
items.text: A convincing email tricks someone into handing over access or running malware.

items.label: Insider
items.text: A careless or malicious employee leaks or takes data they can already reach.

title: Nation-state hackers (APTs)
hook: Patient, well-funded and usually after secrets, not ransom.
what: Advanced Persistent Threats (APTs) are hacking groups backed by governments. They spy, steal intellectual property, pre-position inside critical infrastructure and sometimes sabotage. Security companies give them names (Fancy Bear, Lazarus, Volt Typhoon) and track their tactics. Many 'live off the land', using built-in admin tools so they blend in with normal activity.

example.title: SolarWinds
example.text: Russian intelligence hackers slipped a backdoor into updates for SolarWinds Orion, network software used by about 18,000 organisations, then picked high-value targets including US government agencies.

source.label: Wikipedia: 2020 US federal government data breach

defend: Map defences to attacker behaviour using MITRE ATT&CK
Log and review use of admin tools like PowerShell
Segment networks so one foothold doesn't reach everything
Threat hunting: assume breach and look for it

practice.label: Browse threat groups on MITRE ATT&CK

checks.q: What does 'living off the land' mean?
options: Using a system's own legitimate tools to avoid detection
checks.why: Built-in tools look normal, so defenders watch how they're used, not just whether they run.

checks.q: What does APT stand for?
checks.why: APTs are government-backed groups that spy, steal and pre-position, often staying hidden for a long time.

checks.q: Which framework maps attacker tactics so defenders can check what they'd detect?
checks.why: MITRE ATT&CK catalogues how attackers behave, so teams can map their defences and find the gaps.

items.label: Well-resourced
items.text: Government backing means money, skilled teams and time ordinary criminals don't have.

items.label: Patient
items.text: They stay hidden for months or years (long dwell time), watching and waiting.

items.label: Custom tools
items.text: Bespoke malware and zero-days built for one target, hard to detect with signatures.

items.label: Chosen targets
items.text: Espionage, sabotage or influence against specific governments, firms or infrastructure.

title: DDoS attacks
hook: Knock a site offline by drowning it in traffic.
what: A Distributed Denial of Service attack floods a website or network with so much traffic from so many machines that real users can't get through. The traffic usually comes from botnets of hacked computers, routers and cameras. DDoS is used for extortion, activism (hacktivism), or as a distraction during another attack.

example.title: Mirai and Dyn
example.text: The Mirai botnet infected hundreds of thousands of cameras and routers that still used factory-default passwords, then hit DNS provider Dyn, making Twitter, Netflix, Reddit and others unreachable for parts of a day.

defend: DDoS protection from a CDN or cloud provider
Rate limiting and caching
Change default passwords on every device
A plan for who to call when it happens

checks.q: How did Mirai build such a big botnet?
checks.why: It simply tried a short list of default usernames and passwords.

checks.q: What does 'distributed' mean in DDoS?
options: The traffic comes from many machines at once
It attacks many websites at once
checks.why: The flood comes from many machines, usually a botnet, which is why blocking one source doesn't stop it.

checks.q: Which defence helps most against a large DDoS attack?
options: DDoS protection from a CDN or cloud provider
checks.why: Big providers absorb floods across their global networks before the traffic ever reaches you.

items.label: Volumetric
items.text: Raw bandwidth — fill the pipe with so much traffic nothing else gets through.

items.label: Protocol
items.text: Abuse how connections are set up, like a SYN flood exhausting the server's queue.

items.label: Application-layer
items.text: Cheap-looking requests that are expensive to answer, exhausting the app itself.

items.label: Amplification
items.text: Bounce small spoofed requests off open servers so huge replies hit the victim.

title: AI & security
hook: Deepfakes, prompt injection and AI-powered defence.
what: AI cuts both ways. Attackers use it to write convincing phishing in any language, clone voices and faces for fraud, and speed up finding bugs. AI systems also bring new weaknesses: prompt injection hides instructions in content an AI reads so it does something its user didn't intend, and AI agents with access to tools can be tricked into leaking data. Defenders use AI to sort alerts, analyse malware and spot anomalies faster.

example.title: Arup deepfake call
example.text: An employee at engineering firm Arup joined a video call with what looked like the CFO and colleagues, all of them deepfakes, and was talked into sending about $25 million to criminals.

source.label: CNN Business via ABC17: Arup revealed as $25 million deepfake scam victim

defend: Verify payment requests out-of-band, even on video
Treat anything an AI reads (web pages, emails, files) as untrusted
Give AI agents the least access they need and require approval for risky actions
Follow the OWASP Top 10 for LLM applications

practice.label: Try to trick an AI in Gandalf

checks.q: What is prompt injection?
options: Hiding instructions in content an AI processes to hijack its behaviour
Training an AI on bad data
checks.why: The AI can't reliably tell its user's instructions from text it's reading.

checks.q: Your boss appears on a video call asking for an urgent payment. What's the safe move?
options: Verify through a separate channel you already trust
Ask them to switch the camera on
Pay: you can see their face
checks.why: Faces and voices can be cloned. Check payment requests out-of-band, even on video.

checks.q: Why should an AI agent get only the access it needs?
options: If prompt injection tricks it, the damage it can do is limited
checks.why: Agents can be tricked by instructions hidden in what they read. Least access, plus approval for risky actions, limits the harm.

items.label: Phishing at scale
items.text: Flawless, personalised lures in any language, written in seconds instead of hours.

items.label: Deepfakes
items.text: Cloned voices and video used to impersonate a boss or a family member for fraud.

items.label: Prompt injection
items.text: Hidden instructions in data trick an AI assistant into leaking or acting against its user.

items.label: Defensive AI
items.text: The other side: models that spot anomalies and triage alerts faster than people can.

title: Cloud security
hook: Most cloud breaches are misconfigurations, not clever hacks.
what: In the cloud, the provider secures the infrastructure but you secure what you put on it: the shared responsibility model. The biggest risks are storage buckets left public, over-powered access keys, leaked secrets in code, and identities with far more permissions than they need. Because everything is an API, one stolen key can be as bad as a stolen server room.

example.title: Capital One
example.text: A misconfigured web firewall let an attacker use server-side request forgery (SSRF) to grab cloud credentials from AWS's metadata service, then download data on about 100 million customers.

defend: Least-privilege IAM roles and no long-lived keys
Block public access to storage by default
Scan code repositories for leaked secrets
Enable cloud audit logs and alerts (CloudTrail, Azure Monitor)

practice.label: Play flAWS, an AWS mistakes game

checks.q: Under the shared responsibility model, who secures your S3 bucket permissions?
checks.why: The provider secures the platform; configuration is on you.

checks.q: Which is one of the most common causes of cloud data leaks?
options: Storage buckets left open to the public
checks.why: Most cloud breaches come from customer misconfiguration, such as public buckets and over-powered keys, not the provider.

checks.q: Why is a leaked cloud access key so dangerous?
options: Keys expire the moment they leak
Everything in the cloud is an API, so the key can control resources directly
It only reveals your IP address
checks.why: With the right key, an attacker can create, read or delete resources from anywhere, as if they owned the account.

items.label: Shared responsibility
items.text: The provider secures the hardware and platform; you secure your config, data and access.

items.label: Misconfiguration
items.text: The number-one cloud risk — a setting left open, not a provider being hacked.

items.label: Exposed storage
items.text: A public bucket or database with no authentication, found by anyone scanning.

items.label: Identity & keys
items.text: Leaked API keys and over-permissive roles let one mistake reach everything.

title: Passwords, MFA & passkeys
hook: Identity is the new perimeter.
what: Attackers would rather log in than break in. Passwords get phished, guessed, reused and leaked. Multi-factor authentication (MFA) adds a second proof, but not all MFA is equal: SMS codes can be SIM-swapped, push prompts can be spammed until someone taps Approve (MFA fatigue), and fake login pages can relay codes in real time. Passkeys and hardware security keys are phishing-resistant because they only work on the real website.

example.title: Change Healthcare
example.text: Attackers used stolen credentials on a remote access portal that didn't have MFA. The ransomware attack disrupted pharmacy and insurance payments across the US for weeks.

defend: A password manager with unique passwords everywhere
Passkeys or security keys for important accounts
Number-matching on push MFA to stop fatigue attacks
Alerts on impossible travel and new device logins

checks.q: Why are passkeys considered phishing-resistant?
options: They're tied to the real website's domain and can't be used on a fake one
checks.why: The browser won't release a passkey to a look-alike domain.

checks.q: An attacker sends push MFA prompts over and over until someone taps Approve. What's this called, and what stops it?
options: MFA fatigue; number matching on push prompts
checks.why: MFA fatigue wears people down with prompts. Number matching means approving needs a code from the real login screen.

checks.q: Why are SMS codes weaker than other kinds of MFA?
options: An attacker can take over the phone number with a SIM swap
checks.why: SMS codes can be SIM-swapped or relayed by fake login pages. Passkeys and security keys resist both.

diagram.title: Why a stolen password isn't enough with MFA

steps.text: The password was leaked in a breach or captured by phishing.
The service sends a push prompt, or asks for a code or passkey, to the real owner's device.
The owner wasn't signing in, so they ignore or deny the request.
steps.stop: Number matching stops 'just tap Approve' fatigue attacks.

steps.text: Without the second factor, the password alone gets the attacker nowhere.
steps.stop: Passkeys go further: they only work on the real site, so a fake page gets nothing to replay.

title: IoT & industrial systems
hook: When hacking moves from data to the physical world.
what: IoT means internet-connected devices: cameras, routers, smart TVs. OT (operational technology) and ICS (industrial control systems) run power grids, water plants and factories. These devices often run old software, rarely get patched and were built before anyone expected them to be online. Attacks here can cause physical damage, not just data loss.

example.title: Stuxnet
example.text: A highly sophisticated worm, widely attributed to the US and Israel, sabotaged Iranian uranium centrifuges by changing their speeds while showing operators normal readings. It crossed air-gapped networks via USB drives.

defend: Keep industrial networks separate from office IT
Never expose control systems directly to the internet
Change default credentials and update firmware
Monitor for unexpected commands to controllers

checks.q: Why are OT systems hard to patch?
options: Downtime can stop a factory or utility, and devices may run for decades
checks.why: Availability and safety come first in OT, so changes are planned carefully.

checks.q: What does OT stand for?
checks.why: OT is the technology that runs physical processes: power grids, water plants and factories.

checks.q: What's the most important rule for industrial control systems?
options: Connect them to the office Wi-Fi
Never expose them directly to the internet
checks.why: Control systems were often built before anyone expected them online. Keep them off the internet and separate from office IT.

concept.title: Why these devices are hard to secure

items.label: Weak defaults
items.text: Shipped with default or hard-coded passwords that are rarely changed.

items.label: No updates
items.text: Many never receive patches, so known flaws stay open for years.

items.label: Long lifespans
items.text: Industrial kit runs for decades on software that's long out of support.

items.label: Physical impact
items.text: In OT, a breach can stop a production line or endanger safety, not just data.

title: SQL injection
hook: Talk to the database directly through a login box.
what: Websites store data in databases and ask for it using SQL queries. If a site pastes your input straight into a query, you can change what the query does. Typing ' OR '1'='1 into a login box might turn 'find this user with this password' into 'find any user at all'. It's one of the oldest web bugs and it still causes major breaches.

example.title: MOVEit Transfer
example.text: A SQL injection flaw in this widely used file-transfer product let the Cl0p gang steal data from thousands of organisations in one campaign.

defend: Parameterised queries (prepared statements), always
Least-privilege database accounts
Input validation as a second layer
A web application firewall (WAF) as a safety net

checks.q: What's the real fix for SQL injection?
checks.why: Parameters keep data and code separate, so input can never become part of the query.

checks.q: Why does ' OR '1'='1 work against a vulnerable login form?
options: It makes the query's condition always true, so it matches any user
checks.why: The input closes the quote and adds OR '1'='1, which is always true, so the query returns users without a valid password.

checks.q: What does a least-privilege database account limit?
options: How much damage a successful injection can do
How many users can sign up
checks.why: If the website's database account can only read what it needs, an injection can't drop tables or read everything.

diagram.title: How SQL injection turns a login form against its database

steps.text: Instead of a name, the attacker types text that includes SQL.

steps.msg: SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '' OR '1'='1'
steps.text: The site pastes the input straight into its query, so the attacker's text becomes part of the SQL. '1'='1' is always true.
steps.stop: Parameterised queries keep input as data, never as code. This is the real fix.

steps.text: The database does exactly what the changed query asks.
steps.stop: A least-privilege database account limits what an injection can reach.

steps.msg: Logged in as the first user, often an admin
steps.text: The site treats the result as a successful login.

title: Cross-site scripting (XSS)
hook: Make someone else's browser run your code.
what: XSS happens when a website shows user-supplied content without making it safe, so a script the attacker wrote runs in other visitors' browsers. Because it runs on the real site, it can read what the user sees, act as them and steal session tokens. Stored XSS is saved on the site (like a comment); reflected XSS bounces off a link the victim clicks.

example.title: The Samy worm
example.text: A MySpace user hid a script in his profile that added him as a friend and copied itself to the profile of anyone who viewed it. Over a million people were infected in under a day.

defend: Encode output for where it appears (HTML, attributes, JavaScript)
Use frameworks that escape by default
A strict Content Security Policy
HttpOnly cookies so scripts can't read sessions

checks.q: Where does an XSS payload actually run?
checks.why: That's why it can act as the victim on the trusted site.

checks.q: What's the difference between stored and reflected XSS?
options: Stored targets servers; reflected targets databases
Stored is saved on the site; reflected bounces off a link the victim clicks
checks.why: A stored payload sits on the site, like a comment, and hits every visitor; a reflected one comes from a crafted link.

checks.q: Which cookie setting stops a script from reading the session cookie?
checks.why: HttpOnly cookies are sent to the server but can't be read by JavaScript, so an XSS script can't steal them.

diagram.title: How stored XSS steals a visitor's session

steps.text: The site saves the comment without making it safe.
steps.stop: Encode output for where it appears; use frameworks that escape by default.

steps.text: Everyone who views the comment gets the attacker's script as part of the real page.
steps.stop: A strict Content Security Policy stops inline scripts from running.

steps.msg: Browser runs it and sends the session cookie
steps.text: The script runs in the visitor's browser with the site's permissions.
steps.stop: HttpOnly cookies can't be read by scripts.

steps.msg: Uses the cookie to act as the visitor
steps.text: With the session cookie, the attacker is logged in as the victim.

title: Broken access control & IDOR
hook: Change one number in the URL and see someone else's data.
what: Access control decides who can see and do what. It's #1 on the OWASP Top 10 because it's easy to get wrong. The classic version is IDOR (insecure direct object reference): /invoice/1001 is yours, and changing it to /invoice/1002 shows a stranger's because the app never checks ownership. Others include normal users reaching admin pages or APIs that trust whatever role the browser claims.

example.title: Optus
example.text: Australia's second-largest telco lost personal data on almost 10 million current and former customers. It was widely reported that an internet-facing API needed no login and used sequential customer IDs, though Optus disputed how simple the attack was.

defend: Check permissions on the server for every request
Deny by default
Use unpredictable IDs (but never rely on that alone)
Test with two accounts: can user A see user B's things?

checks.q: Using random IDs instead of 1001, 1002 fully fixes IDOR. True or false?
checks.why: It makes guessing harder, but the real fix is checking ownership on every request.

checks.q: Changing /invoice/1001 to /invoice/1002 shows a stranger's invoice. What's the bug?
options: IDOR: the server never checks who owns the record
checks.why: This is an insecure direct object reference: the app trusts the ID in the URL instead of checking ownership.

checks.q: Where must permission checks happen?
options: On the server, for every request
checks.why: Anything in the browser is under the user's control. Only the server can be trusted to decide who sees what.

items.label: IDOR
items.text: Change an id in the URL (/order/123 → /order/124) and see someone else's data.

items.label: Missing checks
items.text: The server trusts the client to hide a button instead of enforcing the rule itself.

items.label: Forced browsing
items.text: Guess or find a hidden admin URL that was never meant to be reachable.

items.label: Privilege escalation
items.text: A normal user finds a way to act as an admin and do more than they should.

title: Networking basics
hook: IP addresses, ports, DNS: the map every attacker and defender uses.
what: Every device on a network has an IP address, its street address. Ports are the doors on that address: web traffic uses 443 (HTTPS), remote shells use 22 (SSH), Windows remote desktop uses 3389. DNS is the internet's phone book, turning names like example.com into IPs. TCP sets up a reliable conversation with a three-way handshake (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK); UDP just fires packets off. Firewalls decide which doors stay open.

example.title: Exposed RDP
example.text: Remote Desktop (port 3389) left open to the internet with weak passwords has for years been one of the most common ways ransomware gangs get in. Sophos found RDP abused in 90% of the attacks its incident responders handled in 2023. Scanners find exposed RDP within minutes of it going online.

source.label: Sophos: RDP abused in 90% of attacks (2024)

defend: Close every port you don't need
Put remote access behind a VPN or zero-trust gateway with MFA
Segment networks
Monitor DNS. Malware has to phone home somehow.

practice.label: Open real packet captures in Wireshark

checks.q: Which port does HTTPS use by default?
checks.why: 22 is SSH, 53 is DNS, 3389 is RDP.

checks.q: What does DNS do?
options: Turns names like example.com into IP addresses
checks.why: DNS is the internet's phone book: your device asks it for the IP address behind a name.

checks.q: What are the three steps of a TCP handshake?
checks.why: TCP opens a reliable conversation with SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK. (Discover, Offer, Request, Acknowledge is DHCP.)

diagram.title: How a request leaves your network and comes back

steps.text: Your PC knows the site is on another network, so it sends the traffic to its default gateway, the router.
The switch delivers the frame only to the port the router is on.
The router swaps your private IP for its public one (NAT) and sends the packet towards the website's IP, found with DNS.
steps.stop: A firewall here decides which traffic may pass.

steps.text: The website answers to the router's public IP, and the router hands it back to your PC.

title: Encryption & hashing
hook: Locks, keys and fingerprints for data.
what: Encryption scrambles data so only someone with the key can read it. Symmetric encryption (AES) uses one shared key. Asymmetric encryption (RSA, elliptic curve) uses a public key to lock and a private key to unlock, which is how HTTPS starts a secure connection with a site you've never met. Hashing is different: it's a one-way fingerprint. You can't reverse it, so sites store password hashes, ideally with slow algorithms like bcrypt or Argon2 plus a unique salt.

example.title: LinkedIn
example.text: In 2012 about 6.5 million LinkedIn password hashes were posted online; in 2016 it emerged the same breach covered about 117 million accounts. The hashes used SHA-1 with no salt, so attackers cracked most of them quickly with precomputed tables.

defend: Use TLS everywhere
Hash passwords with bcrypt, scrypt or Argon2 and a salt
Never write your own crypto; use vetted libraries
Protect and rotate keys (key management is the hard part)

practice.label: Learn by breaking crypto on CryptoHack

checks.q: Why do sites hash passwords instead of encrypting them?
options: Hashes can't be turned back into the password, so a leak reveals less
checks.why: The site only needs to check a match, never read the original.

checks.q: Which kind of encryption uses a public key to lock and a private key to unlock?
options: Asymmetric, such as RSA or elliptic curve
checks.why: Asymmetric encryption is how HTTPS starts a secure connection with a site you've never met. Then both sides switch to a fast shared key.

checks.q: Why should each password hash use a unique salt?
options: So the hash can be reversed later
So identical passwords get different hashes and precomputed tables don't work
checks.why: A salt is random data added before hashing, so attackers can't crack many identical passwords at once with ready-made tables.

diagram.title: How HTTPS (TLS) protects you on shared Wi-Fi

steps.text: Your browser starts a TLS connection and offers the encryption methods it supports.
The server sends a certificate signed by a trusted authority, so you know it's the real site.
Both sides work out the same secret key using public-key maths, without ever sending the key itself.
Everything after that, such as your password and balance, is encrypted with the shared key. The eavesdropper only sees scrambled bytes.
steps.stop: Use TLS everywhere, and never click through certificate warnings.

title: Linux command line
hook: Most servers and most security tools live here.
what: Most of the internet runs on Linux, and most security tools are built for it. Core commands to know: ls (list files), cd (move), cat and less (read files), grep (search text), find (search files), ps and top (running processes), ss or netstat (network connections), chmod and chown (permissions), sudo (run as admin). Logs live in /var/log. Pipes (|) chain commands together, and that's where the real power is.

example.title: Log triage
example.text: A SOC analyst can find brute-force attempts in seconds: grep "Failed password" /var/log/auth.log | awk '{print $(NF-3)}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr lists the IPs with the most failed SSH logins.

defend: Disable SSH password logins; use keys
Run services as unprivileged users
Keep packages updated
Ship logs somewhere attackers can't delete them

checks.q: Which command searches inside files for text?
checks.why: find searches for files by name; grep searches their contents.

checks.q: Where do most Linux logs live?
checks.why: System and security logs, such as auth.log for logins, are kept under /var/log.

checks.q: What does a pipe (|) do?
options: Sends one command's output into the next command
checks.why: Pipes chain commands together, for example grep Failed auth.log | wc -l counts failed logins.

items.label: Move around
items.text: pwd (where am I), ls (list), cd (change directory), find (locate files).

items.label: Read files
items.text: cat and less (view), grep (search text), head and tail (first/last lines).

items.label: Permissions
items.text: chmod (change permissions), chown (change owner), sudo (run as admin).

items.label: Processes
items.text: ps and top (what's running), kill (stop it), systemctl (manage services).

items.label: Network
items.text: ip and ifconfig (interfaces), ping (reach a host), ss (open ports).

title: The SOC, SIEM & logs
hook: Where most cyber careers start.
what: A Security Operations Center (SOC) is the team that watches for attacks around the clock. Logs from servers, laptops, firewalls and cloud services flow into a SIEM (Security Information and Event Management) tool such as Splunk, Microsoft Sentinel or Elastic, where detection rules raise alerts. Analysts triage each alert: is it real, how bad is it, and what's affected? Most alerts are false positives, so the skill is investigating quickly and calmly.

example.title: Target
example.text: Target's security tools actually alerted on the malware that went on to steal 40 million card numbers, but the alerts weren't acted on. Detection only works if someone responds.

source.label: The Register: Target failed to act on security alerts

defend: Collect the right logs (authentication, process creation, DNS, EDR)
Tune detections to cut false positives
Write playbooks for common alerts
Use MITRE ATT&CK to find coverage gaps

checks.q: What does a SIEM mainly do?
options: Collects and correlates logs to raise alerts
checks.why: It gives analysts one place to search and detect across everything.

checks.q: Most alerts turn out to be false positives. What does that mean for an analyst?
options: Triage fast: is it real, how bad is it, what's affected?
checks.why: The skill is investigating quickly and calmly so the real incidents get attention.

checks.q: Which logs matter most to collect for detection?
options: Authentication, process creation, DNS and EDR
checks.why: These show who logged in, what ran, where devices connected and what endpoint protection saw.

diagram.title: How a SOC turns logs into a response

steps.msg: Logs: 30 failed logins, then a success
steps.text: Laptops, servers and cloud services send their logs to the SIEM.
A detection rule matches the pattern and raises an alert.
Which account? From where? What happened after the login? Most alerts are false positives, so triage is quick.

steps.msg: Contains: disables the account, isolates the laptop
steps.text: If it's real, the analyst contains it first and keeps the evidence.
steps.stop: Playbooks make the response fast and consistent.

title: Incident response
hook: What to do in the worst hour of the year.
what: Incident response (IR) is the plan for when something goes wrong. The classic phases: Preparation, Detection & Analysis, Containment, Eradication, Recovery, and Lessons Learned. The first instinct, wiping the machine, can destroy evidence. Good IR teams contain first (isolate the host, disable the account), preserve evidence, find the root cause and then rebuild. Clear communication matters as much as technical skill.

example.title: CrowdStrike outage
example.text: Not an attack: a faulty security update crashed about 8.5 million Windows machines worldwide. It showed that IR plans need to cover outages and recovery at scale, not just hackers.

defend: Write and rehearse a plan before you need it (tabletop exercises)
Know who to call: legal, comms, insurers, law enforcement
Keep offline copies of critical contacts and runbooks
Run a blameless post-incident review

practice.label: Work through incident labs on CyberDefenders

checks.q: You find malware on a laptop. What should usually come first?
options: Isolate it from the network and preserve evidence
checks.why: Containment stops the spread; evidence tells you how they got in.

checks.q: Why can wiping an infected machine straight away be a mistake?
options: It destroys evidence you need to find the root cause
checks.why: Contain first and preserve evidence; otherwise you may never learn how the attacker got in, and they'll come back.

checks.q: What's the final phase of the classic incident response cycle?
checks.why: The cycle ends with a blameless review so the same incident doesn't happen again.

items.label: Prepare
items.text: Plans, contacts, tooling and practice drills in place before anything happens.

items.label: Identify
items.text: Detect and confirm it's a real incident, and work out its scope.

items.label: Contain
items.text: Stop the bleeding — isolate affected systems so it can't spread.

items.label: Eradicate
items.text: Remove the attacker and the malware, and close the way they got in.

items.label: Recover
items.text: Restore clean systems and watch closely to be sure the threat is gone.

items.label: Lessons learned
items.text: Write up what happened and fix the gaps so it doesn't recur. Feeds back into Prepare.

title: OSINT
hook: Finding out a lot from what's already public.
what: Open-Source Intelligence means gathering information from public sources: websites, social media, job ads, DNS records, code repositories, breach dumps and photo metadata. Attackers use it to plan phishing and find exposed systems. Defenders use it to see their organisation the way attackers do. Ethical OSINT stays on public information and respects privacy: you investigate organisations and threats, not stalk individuals.

example.title: Job ads as recon
example.text: A job posting asking for 'experience with Fortinet VPN and Citrix' tells an attacker exactly which products to look up vulnerabilities for.

defend: Audit what your organisation exposes publicly
Strip metadata from published files and photos
Train staff on oversharing
Monitor for leaked credentials and code

checks.q: Which of these is ethical OSINT practice?
options: Logging in to someone's account with a guessed password
Reviewing your company's public DNS records and job ads
checks.why: OSINT uses public information only and has a legitimate purpose.

checks.q: How do defenders use OSINT?
options: To see their organisation the way attackers do
checks.why: Looking at what's publicly exposed shows defenders what an attacker would find first.

checks.q: A photo you publish contains GPS metadata. What's the risk, and the fix?
options: It can reveal where it was taken; strip metadata before publishing
It slows your website; compress it
checks.why: Photo metadata can include location and device details. Strip it from files and photos before they go public.

items.label: Search & dorking
items.text: Targeted search queries surface exposed files, logins and documents.

items.label: Social media
items.text: Names, roles, locations and habits people post publicly, useful for pretexting.

items.label: DNS & WHOIS
items.text: Domains, subdomains and registration data map an organisation's footprint.

items.label: Breach data
items.text: Credentials from past breaches, checked against sites like Have I Been Pwned.

items.label: Public records
items.text: Company filings, certificates and job ads that reveal tech and structure.
